explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. The text says she learned Jesus was dining there and brought an alabaster jar of perfume (Luke 7:37). Remember that jar, because it's about to matter. Me, I'd have walked in with a box of cookies and been WAY too proud of myself.

I get the mix-up, friend. Minty, one of my cookie cutter kids, is shaped like a dove, so doves are always on my mind. But the text never puts a bird in her hands. It says she brought an alabaster jar of perfume (Luke 7:37).

A bag of silver does sound like a gift with some weight to it. But nothing in this verse jingles. The text says she brought an alabaster jar of perfume (Luke 7:37). Jar. Perfume. That's the whole shopping list.
True. She began to wet His feet with her tears and wipe them with her hair (Luke 7:38). No towel is mentioned, just her hair. I think she gave Him what she had right there with her.

The text says she began to wet His feet with her tears and wipe them with her hair (Luke 7:38). So it's her own hair, not a towel or a cloth. Nobody hands her a napkin in this scene. Hair is the only thing named.

explanations.answer: She anoints His feet with it
explanations.explanation: Right, friend. She kissed His feet and then anointed them with the perfume (Luke 7:38). Feet, not head. The text has her standing behind Him at His feet.

explanations.answer: She pours it over His head
explanations.explanation: The head is a fair guess, friend, but the text puts the perfume on His feet. She kissed His feet and anointed them with the perfume (Luke 7:38). Her tears and her hair are already at His feet in that same verse.

explanations.answer: She hands it to the Pharisee
explanations.explanation: Handing the jar to Simon would be a very different story, friend. The text says she anointed His feet with the perfume (Luke 7:38). Nothing in that verse has her handing it to anyone. Simon is busy in his own head, which we're about to hear about.

True. The Pharisee says to himself, “If this man were a prophet, He would know who this is and what kind of woman is touching Him…” (Luke 7:39). He never says it out loud. It's all happening inside his head.

The text says the Pharisee did say this to himself. He thinks, “If this man were a prophet, He would know who this is and what kind of woman is touching Him…” (Luke 7:39). Keep that in mind for the next verse.
True. The Pharisee only said it to himself, but the text says Jesus answered him (Luke 7:40). It doesn't say how Jesus knew. It just says He spoke up, and Simon heard it.

The text says Jesus did answer him, even though the Pharisee only spoke to himself. Jesus says, “Simon, I have something to tell you.” (Luke 7:40). The text doesn't explain how Jesus knew. It just shows Him answering.
Not quite, baker. After Jesus says He has something to tell him, Simon answers, “Tell me, Teacher…” (Luke 7:40). That's a man opening the door, not slamming it. He's ready to hear it.
False is right. Simon says, “Tell me, Teacher…” (Luke 7:40). He asks to hear what Jesus has to say. Whatever was running through his head a minute ago, he leans in.
Fifty is right. One man owed five hundred denarii and the other fifty (Luke 7:41). Two debts, and a big gap between them. Hold on to that gap, because Jesus is about to use it.

Forty is close, friend, but the text says fifty. One owed five hundred denarii and the other fifty (Luke 7:41). It's an easy one to slip on when the numbers start rolling. I've overcounted a tray of cookies the same way.

Ten would be a much smaller debt than the one in the text. The second man owed fifty denarii, and the first owed five hundred (Luke 7:41). Still a gap between them, just not as wide as you picked. Count again and you'll land on fifty.
That's not what the text says, friend. When neither man could repay, the moneylender forgave both of them. The text says “…he forgave both of them.” (Luke 7:42). Nobody gets left holding the bill.

False is right. When the two men were unable to repay, the text says “…he forgave both of them.” (Luke 7:42). The man with the smaller debt and the man with the bigger debt both walk away forgiven. That's the setup for the question coming next.

explanations.answer: The one who was forgiven more
explanations.explanation: Simon says, “I suppose the one who was forgiven more…” (Luke 7:43). Listen to that little “I suppose.” I think he can feel something coming and wants to answer carefully. And he picks the right one.

explanations.answer: The one who was forgiven less
explanations.explanation: That's the opposite of what Simon says. He answers, “I suppose the one who was forgiven more…” (Luke 7:43). The man who owed five hundred had more wiped away. That's the man Simon names.

explanations.answer: Both of them about the same
explanations.explanation: Simon doesn't call it a tie. He says, “I suppose the one who was forgiven more…” (Luke 7:43). He picks one man, the one who owed more. No fence-sitting.
True. Jesus tells him, “You have judged correctly…” (Luke 7:43). Simon gets the answer right. Keep an eye on where Jesus takes it from here.
The text says Jesus tells him, “You have judged correctly…” (Luke 7:43). Simon's answer was right on the money. Jesus has more to say, but He starts by saying Simon got that one right.

That's it. Jesus says, “When I entered your house, you did not give Me water for My feet, but she wet My feet with her tears and wiped them with her hair.” (Luke 7:44). Water for the feet is the first thing on His list. The woman's tears do what the water didn't.

The text says Jesus reclined at the table (Luke 7:36), so He did have a place. What Simon did not give Him was water for His feet (Luke 7:44). Seat yes, foot water no. Check Jesus' list again and that one pops right out.

Simon did invite Him. The text opens with the Pharisee inviting Jesus to eat with him (Luke 7:36). What he didn't give was water for His feet (Luke 7:44). He got Jesus through the door, but the little welcome touches were missing.

That's not what Jesus says. He tells Simon, “You did not greet Me with a kiss, but she has not stopped kissing My feet since I arrived.” (Luke 7:45). Simon gets no kiss in that line. The kissing Jesus describes comes from the woman.

False is right. Jesus says, “You did not greet Me with a kiss, but she has not stopped kissing My feet since I arrived.” (Luke 7:45). Simon did not greet Him with a kiss. The woman has not stopped kissing His feet.
Head is the first blank. Jesus says, “You did not anoint My head with oil…” (Luke 7:46). That's what Simon didn't do. Well done, friend.
Feet fills the second blank. Jesus says “…but she has anointed My feet with perfume.” (Luke 7:46). Head for Simon's missing oil, feet for her perfume.

Hands don't show up in either half of this verse. Jesus names the head for Simon's missing oil and the feet for the woman's perfume (Luke 7:46). Hands never come up. Check the two body parts He actually names.

The face isn't in this verse, friend. Jesus says Simon did not anoint His head with oil, and the woman anointed His feet with perfume (Luke 7:46). Two spots, head and feet. The face just isn't on the list.

No beard in this verse, friend. Jesus names the head for the oil Simon didn't give and the feet for the perfume the woman did (Luke 7:46). Beard never comes up. Check the two body parts He actually names.

That's what He says. “…her many sins have been forgiven, for she has loved much.” (Luke 7:47). It lines up with the story of the two debtors, where the one forgiven more was the one who would love more. Jesus ties her story right back to it.
Giving is a good guess, since she brought that jar. But that's not the word Jesus uses. He says “…her many sins have been forgiven, for she has loved much.” (Luke 7:47). The word is loved.

The text never says anything about her praying, friend. What Jesus says is “…her many sins have been forgiven, for she has loved much.” (Luke 7:47). Loved is the word He picks. Everything she did in that house, He points to as love.
True. Jesus says, “…he who has been forgiven little loves little.” (Luke 7:47). It's the other half of what He says about the woman. Same story of the two debtors, now pointed right at Simon's table.

The text says He does say it. Jesus says, “…he who has been forgiven little loves little.” (Luke 7:47). It's the second half of that verse, right after He says the woman has loved much. Both halves are right there in His words.

explanations.answer: Who is this who even forgives sins
explanations.explanation: That's what they say. “Who is this who even forgives sins?” (Luke 7:49). It happens right after Jesus tells the woman her sins are forgiven. The text doesn't say what they decide.

explanations.answer: Why does He let this woman stay
explanations.explanation: That's a fair thing to wonder at a table like this, friend. But the text doesn't have them say it. What they say to themselves is “Who is this who even forgives sins?” (Luke 7:49). Their question is about Jesus Himself.

explanations.answer: How does He know what Simon thinks
explanations.explanation: Good question, and I wondered it too. But the text doesn't have them ask it. They say to themselves, “Who is this who even forgives sins?” (Luke 7:49). It comes right after Jesus tells the woman her sins are forgiven.

True. The text says that as Jesus travels from town to town, “The Twelve were with Him…” (Luke 8:1). He's preaching and proclaiming the good news of the kingdom of God, and they're right there with Him. That's a full road trip.
The text says the opposite. Luke 8:1 says, “The Twelve were with Him…” as He traveled from one town and village to another. So the apostles are along for the trip.
Seven is right. The text says “Mary called Magdalene, from whom seven demons had gone out…” (Luke 8:2). She's named as one of the women who had been healed. Quite a story behind that name.
Two is a lot short, friend. The text says seven demons had gone out of Mary called Magdalene (Luke 8:2). That's how the verse tells you how much she'd been through. Seven.

Twelve is an easy slip, since the Twelve are mentioned in the verse right before this one (Luke 8:1). But for Mary called Magdalene, the text says seven demons had gone out (Luke 8:2). Twelve belongs to the apostles. Seven belongs to Mary.

explanations.answer: Providing for them from their own resources
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. The text says, “These women were ministering to them out of their own means.” (Luke 8:3). Joanna, Susanna and many others were helping with what they had.

explanations.answer: Sending word ahead to each new town
explanations.explanation: Sending word ahead isn't what the text says about these women. It says, “These women were ministering to them out of their own means.” (Luke 8:3). Nothing in that verse mentions sending word ahead.

explanations.answer: Teaching the crowds in each village
explanations.explanation: Teaching the crowds isn't what the text says about these women. Luke 8:1 has Jesus preaching and proclaiming the good news. About the women it says, “These women were ministering to them out of their own means.” (Luke 8:3).
